body:
The evidence base is real but narrower than the marketing. **Cross-sectional momentum** (Jegadeesh & Titman: ~1% a month for 3–12-month winners) and the **52-week-high effect** are among the most robust anomalies in finance. Nearness to the 52-week high explains much of momentum and does not reverse, and it appears in 18 of 20 international markets ([George & Hwang 2004](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2004.00695.x); [CXO Advisory](https://www.cxoadvisory.com/1284/technical-trading/the-52-week-high-as-a-momentum-indicator-for-individual-stocks/)). **Post-earnings-announcement drift**, where stocks keep drifting about 60 days after big surprises, underpins CAN SLIM's "C" and Qullamaggie's Episodic Pivots ([Bernard & Thomas 1989](https://doi.org/10.2307/2491062)). Momentum also works in India. Profits are concentrated in the winners (the long leg) and are not explained by CAPM or Fama-French ([Ansari & Khan 2012](https://emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/03074351211193730/full/html)). That matters because long-only cash investors keep most of the edge. Momentum does suffer **rare, violent crashes** when markets rebound sharply after a panic ([Daniel & Moskowitz 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2015.12.002)). Market-regime filters exist to manage that risk. Specific chart shapes, such as exact cup depths and handle lengths, have weak, data-snooping-sensitive evidence. Park & Irwin's survey found positive results in 56 of 95 studies, but many had methodological problems, and the evidence is stronger in older samples ([Park & Irwin 2007](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-6419.2007.00519.x)). The defensible conclusion is that patterns are **timing and risk-definition tools, not alpha sources**. The practitioners themselves credit their risk rules.

For Indian investors, the most rule-based implementation is the **Nifty200 Momentum 30** index. It holds the top 30 Nifty 200 stocks by volatility-adjusted 6- and 12-month returns and rebalances in June and December ([NSE factsheet](https://www.niftyindices.com/Factsheet/Factsheet_Nifty200_Momentum30.pdf)). Turnover is heavy: **19 of 30 names changed in the December 2025 rebalance** ([Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/markets/news/nifty200-momentum30-a-flip-of-index-switch-jolts-16k-cr-across-the-grid-125121400388_1.html)). Chartink, MarketInOut, Sharpely and Screener host ready-made Minervini/Stage-2 scans ([MarketInOut Trend Template India](https://www.marketinout.com/stock-screener/minervini-trend-template/india); [Screener "Mark minervini"](https://www.screener.in/screens/672150/mark-minervini)). The Indian adaptation needs a **liquidity floor**, for example ₹5–10 crore of daily traded value. Circuit limits on small caps can lock you in, and your stop may never execute.

body:
Research notes, compiled 2026-11-19. They are written for a retail investor in India who also buys US stocks.

**How to read these notes.** "Said" means the investor's own words or primary documents, such as shareholder letters, books and fund materials. "Commentary" means summaries by third parties, such as blogs, brokers and podcasts. Some sources were opened or surfaced in this session through search; for those, the search snippets were read. Other citations are well-known primary documents (Berkshire letters, classic books) cited from prior knowledge and **not re-fetched this session**. Each of these is marked **[primary, not re-fetched]**. Check the exact wording before quoting any of them in a published report.

data.section: Fundamental Stock-Picking Frameworks of Legendary Investors and the Valuation Metrics They Use

title: fundamental_frameworks › Fundamental Stock-Picking Frameworks of Legendary Investors and the Valuation Metrics They Use

body:
**Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway letters)**
- **Four filters (said).** Berkshire wants a business "(1) that we can understand; (2) with favorable long-term prospects; (3) operated by honest and competent people; and (4) available at a very attractive price." — [1977 Berkshire letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1977.html) [primary, not re-fetched]
- **Acquisition criteria (said).** These are printed in each annual report:
  - "demonstrated consistent earning power (future projections are of no interest to us, nor are 'turnaround' situations)"
  - "businesses earning good returns on equity while employing little or no debt"
  - "management in place"
  - "simple businesses (if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it)"
  - "an offering price"
  - Source: [Berkshire annual letters, e.g. 1997](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1997.html) [primary, not re-fetched]
- **Owner earnings (said).** Buffett defines owner earnings as "(a) reported earnings plus (b) depreciation, depletion, amortization, and certain other non-cash charges ... less (c) the average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment, etc. that the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and its unit volume." The formula is therefore Net income + D&A + other non-cash charges − maintenance capex (± any working capital the business needs to hold its position). — [1986 Berkshire letter (appendix on Scott Fetzer purchase accounting)](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1986.html) [primary, not re-fetched]
- **Wonderful company at a fair price (said).** "It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price." — [1989 Berkshire letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1989.html) [primary, not re-fetched]
- **Circle of competence (said).** Buffett's ideal is to buy "at a rational price, a part interest in an easily-understandable business whose earnings are virtually certain to be materially higher five, ten and twenty years from now." On the circle of competence: "The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital." — [1996 Berkshire letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1996.html) [primary, not re-fetched]
- **Moats (said).** "A truly great business must have an enduring 'moat' that protects excellent returns on invested capital." In the same letter Buffett sorts businesses into "great, good, gruesome". See's Candies is the great example: it needs little capital to grow. — [2007 Berkshire letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2007ltr.pdf) [primary, not re-fetched]
- **Intrinsic value and growth (said).** Intrinsic value is the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business over its remaining life. Buffett says growth and value are "joined at the hip": growth only adds value when the return on incremental capital is above its cost. — [1992 Berkshire letter](https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1992.html) [primary, not re-fetched]
title: fundamental_frameworks › Cited Findings

body:
- How to reframe "certainty" for a retail reader:
  - A good bet has positive expected value: p(win) × upside − p(loss) × downside > 0.
  - Because a few big winners drive most returns (Bessembinder), let winners run and cut thesis-broken losers.
  - Even a 55–60% hit rate is elite.
- Worked sizing example (illustrative arithmetic only): a 60% chance of +50% against a 40% chance of −25% gives EV = 0.6×0.5 − 0.4×0.25 = +20%. Kelly f* = p/a − q/b = 0.6/0.25 − 0.4/0.5 = 1.6, i.e. 160% of capital, which is absurd. That shows why pros use ¼–½ Kelly and hard position caps (e.g., 5–10%), given that the probability estimates themselves are unreliable.
- Sell discipline pros use: (1) the thesis or kill criterion is breached, (2) the variant perception has been priced in (Steinhardt), (3) a better risk/reward exists, and (4) position-size limits are hit. A price drop alone is not a reason, unless the thesis was timing-based.
title: institutional_process › Inferences

body:
**D-Mart: founding and retail model**
- 1997/1999: took an Apna Bazaar cooperative franchise (Nerul). Sources give 1997 and 1999. He was unconvinced by its model, and it shaped his view of the target customer. — [Outlook Business](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/lead-story/radhakishan-damani-the-slow-and-steady-retail-king-6675); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radhakishan_Damani)
- About 2000: he reportedly left the stock market and bought cheap land in Navi Mumbai. First store opened in Powai in 2002 (Rediff says 2003). 25 stores by 2010. — [Rediff](https://www.rediff.com/business/special/how-well-do-you-know-d-marts-damani/20170405.htm); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radhakishan_Damani)
- Deliberately slow rollout: about a decade in, Big Bazaar had roughly 250 stores to D-Mart's 10. The model is perfected in one cluster, then extended to adjacent catchments and cities. — [Outlook Business](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/lead-story/radhakishan-damani-the-slow-and-steady-retail-king-6675)
- The model: everyday low prices, about 8% below retail daily rather than through sales events. It owns store properties instead of leasing; mall rent plus maintenance can be about 7% of revenue and rises about 5% a year. No-frills stores, a narrow grocery and general-merchandise range, 3-4x the inventory turns of peers, and vendors paid within about 10 days, which wins better FMCG terms. — [Outlook Business](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/lead-story/radhakishan-damani-the-slow-and-steady-retail-king-6675)
- FY16 profit after tax was ₹318 crore with 23.6% ROE, against 3.6% at the next-best peer (Trent). The March 2017 IPO was subscribed 145 times and the stock roughly doubled on listing. His roughly 82% stake was worth more than ₹32,000 crore. — [Rediff](https://www.rediff.com/business/special/how-well-do-you-know-d-marts-damani/20170405.htm). It listed at a 102% premium (₹604.4 open, about ₹39,988 crore market cap). — [Business Today](https://www.businesstoday.in/markets/stocks/rakesh-jhunjunwala-guru-radhakishan-damani-second-richest-mukesh-ambani/story/396422.html)
- Net worth: Forbes ranked him 98th in India in 2015 at $1.15bn (pre-IPO), and he jumped once D-Mart listed. 2026 estimates range from $13.7bn (Forbes real-time, 10 Nov 2026) to $15.7bn (Forbes 2026 list). He was $31.5bn in October 2024, so the fall since then tracks D-Mart's de-rating. — [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radhakishan_Damani); [Powerbase](https://powerbase.info/index.php/Radhakishan_Damani); [Lemonn](https://lemonn.co.in/blog/bytes/richest-people-in-india/)

body:
**Legal limits (SEBI PIT Regulations 2015):** UPSI = information about a company or its securities, not generally available, that would likely materially affect the price on becoming available [Reg 2(1)(n)]. It includes financial results, dividends, change in capital structure, M&A/delisting/disposals and KMP changes. "Generally available" = accessible to the public on a non-discriminatory basis [Reg 2(1)(e)]. The May-2024 amendment excludes *unverified* media reports from that. An "insider" is anyone in possession of UPSI, *however obtained*, so a channel check that extracts unreleased quarterly sales from a company employee makes the investor an insider. Trading while in possession is prohibited [Reg 4]; procuring or communicating UPSI is prohibited [Reg 3]. Safe practice:
1. Ask about **your own observations and the counter-party's own business** (a dealer's own stock and sales are the dealer's information, not the listed company's UPSI). Never ask an employee about unreleased company numbers, orders, deals or results.
2. If someone volunteers UPSI, **stop, write it down, and do not trade** that stock until the information is public.
3. Don't pay employees for information. Paid expert-network calls with current employees carry high risk.
4. Keep a dated scuttlebutt log of who, what and when (that is part of the memdb record) to show the mosaic was built from public pieces.
Sources: [KPMG on UPSI](https://assets.kpmg.com/content/dam/kpmg/in/pdf/2020/02/Safeguarding-UPSI.pdf), [Vinod Kothari PIT FAQ](https://vinodkothari.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/FAQs_Primer-on-PIT-Regulations_ver-20.08.2021.pdf), [Chambers on 2024 amendment](https://chambers.com/articles/amendments-to-the-sebi-prohibition-of-insider-trading-regulations-2015-widening-the-scope-of-un). This is not legal advice; India has no formal "mosaic theory" safe harbour, so treat this conservatively.
